chapter_name: 002 - II - Suddenly I found myself lying awake, peering from my sandy mattress
source_text:
II.


Suddenly I found myself lying awake, peering from my sandy mattress
through the door of the tent. I looked at my watch pinned against the
canvas, and saw by the bright moonlight that it was past twelve
o’clock—the threshold of a new day—and I had therefore slept a couple
of hours. The Swede was asleep still beside me; the wind howled as
before; something plucked at my heart and made me feel afraid. There
was a sense of disturbance in my immediate neighborhood.

I sat up quickly and looked out. The trees were swaying violently to
and fro as the gusts smote them, but our little bit of green canvas lay
snugly safe in the hollow, for the wind passed over it without meeting
enough resistance to make it vicious. The feeling of disquietude did
not pass, however, and I crawled quietly out of the tent to see if our
belongings were safe. I moved carefully so as not to waken my
companion. A curious excitement was on me.

I was half-way out, kneeling on all fours, when my eye first took in
that the tops of the bushes opposite, with their moving tracery of
leaves, made shapes against the sky. I sat back on my haunches and
stared. It was incredible, surely, but there, opposite and slightly
above me, were shapes of some indeterminate sort among the willows, and
as the branches swayed in the wind they seemed to group themselves
about these shapes, forming a series of monstrous outlines that shifted
rapidly beneath the moon. Close, about fifty feet in front of me, I saw
these things.

My first instinct was to waken my companion, that he too might see
them, but something made me hesitate—the sudden realization, probably,
that I should not welcome corroboration; and meanwhile I crouched there
staring in amazement with smarting eyes. I was wide awake. I remember
saying to myself that I was _not_ dreaming.

They first became properly visible, these huge figures, just within the
tops of the bushes—immense, bronze-colored, moving, and wholly
independent of the swaying of the branches. I saw them plainly and
noted, now I came to examine them more calmly, that they were very much
larger than human, and indeed that something in their appearance
proclaimed them to be _not human_ at all. Certainly they were not
merely the moving tracery of the branches against the moonlight. They
shifted independently. They rose upwards in a continuous stream from
earth to sky, vanishing utterly as soon as they reached the dark of the
sky. They were interlaced one with another, making a great column, and
I saw their limbs and huge bodies melting in and out of each other,
forming this serpentine line that bent and swayed and twisted spirally
with the contortions of the wind-tossed trees. They were nude, fluid
shapes, passing up the bushes, _within_ the leaves almost—rising up in
a living column into the heavens. Their faces I never could see.
Unceasingly they poured upwards, swaying in great bending curves, with
a hue of dull bronze upon their skins.

I stared, trying to force every atom of vision from my eyes. For a long
time I thought they _must_ every moment disappear and resolve
themselves into the movements of the branches and prove to be an
optical illusion. I searched everywhere for a proof of reality, when
all the while I understood quite well that the standard of reality had
changed. For the longer I looked the more certain I became that these
figures were real and living, though perhaps not according to the
standards that the camera and the biologist would insist upon.

Far from feeling fear, I was possessed with a sense of awe and wonder
such as I have never known. I seemed to be gazing at the personified
elemental forces of this haunted and primeval region. Our intrusion had
stirred the powers of the place into activity. It was we who were the
cause of the disturbance, and my brain filled to bursting with stories
and legends of the spirits and deities of places that have been
acknowledged and worshipped by men in all ages of the world’s history.
But, before I could arrive at any possible explanation, something
impelled me to go farther out, and I crept forward on the sand and
stood upright. I felt the ground still warm under my bare feet; the
wind tore at my hair and face; and the sound of the river burst upon my
ears with a sudden roar. These things, I knew, were real, and proved
that my senses were acting normally. Yet the figures still rose from
earth to heaven, silent, majestically, in a great spiral of grace and
strength that overwhelmed me at length with a genuine deep emotion of
worship. I felt that I must fall down and worship—absolutely worship.

Perhaps in another minute I might have done so, when a gust of wind
swept against me with such force that it blew me sideways, and I nearly
stumbled and fell. It seemed to shake the dream violently out of me. At
least it gave me another point of view somehow. The figures still
remained, still ascended into heaven from the heart of the night, but
my reason at last began to assert itself. It must be a subjective
experience, I argued—none the less real for that, but still subjective.
The moonlight and the branches combined to work out these pictures upon
the mirror of my imagination, and for some reason I projected them
outwards and made them appear objective. I knew this must be the case,
of course. I took courage, and began to move forward across the open
patches of sand. By Jove, though, was it all hallucination? Was it
merely subjective? Did not my reason argue in the old futile way from
the little standard of the known?

I only know that great column of figures ascended darkly into the sky
for what seemed a very long period of time, and with a very complete
measure of reality as most men are accustomed to gauge reality. Then
suddenly they were gone!

And, once they were gone and the immediate wonder of their great
presence had passed, fear came down upon me with a cold rush. The
esoteric meaning of this lonely and haunted region suddenly flamed up
within me, and I began to tremble dreadfully. I took a quick look
round—a look of horror that came near to panic—calculating vainly ways
of escape; and then, realizing how helpless I was to achieve anything
really effective, I crept back silently into the tent and lay down
again upon my sandy mattress, first lowering the door-curtain to shut
out the sight of the willows in the moonlight, and then burying my head
as deeply as possible beneath the blankets to deaden the sound of the
terrifying wind.

My wristwatch, pinned haphazardly against the canvas, glowed under the pale light of the full moon. Beside me, the Swede lay in a fitful slumber, his breathing heavy and ragged like the gale that howled relentlessly around us. But the wind alone could not explain the chill crawling up my spine, nor the frantic hammering of my own heart. Something was wrong here, in this immediate circle of darkness, a disturbance that vibrated in the air like a plucked string.

I threw off the covers and scrambled to the edge of the tent, peering out into the chaos. The trees were thrashing, their branches whipping back and forth as the gusts battered them with brutal force. Yet, miraculously, our small patch of green canvas remained anchored, nestled safely in the hollow, unscathed by the fury above. The wind roared over it, offering no resistance strong enough to tear it away. Still, the unease gnawed at me, a cold knot in my gut that refused to loosen. I crawled out of the tent, moving with deliberate silence so as not to rouse my sleeping companion, driven by a strange, electric excitement that made my skin prickle.

Halfway out, dropping to my knees on the coarse sand, I froze. My gaze caught the tops of the bushes directly opposite, their leafy tracery dancing wildly against the black sky. I sat back on my heels, staring, unable to breathe. It was impossible, yet there, standing amidst the willows and slightly elevated above them, were shapes. As the branches swayed, these forms seemed to coalesce, arranging themselves into grotesque, shifting silhouettes that twisted rapidly beneath the lunar glare. They were close, perhaps fifty feet away, looming out of the gloom.

My first, reflexive urge was to wake the Swede, to share this vision, but a sudden, paralyzing hesitation stopped me. Some primal voice whispered that I would not welcome confirmation from anyone else—that the truth needed to remain mine alone. So, I crouched there, staring in a daze, my eyes stinging with the strain of seeing what I dared not fully believe. *Not a dream,* I told myself, the words echoing in the hollow space of my mind. *I am wide awake.*

Then, slowly, the impossible became clear. These were not mere shadows cast by the swaying boughs. Emerging from behind the brush, towering immense and colossal, were figures of a bronze, metallic hue. They moved with a jerky, fluid independence, entirely separate from the chaotic dance of the trees. As I watched, mesmerized, I noted with growing horror that they were far larger than any man, and their proportions defied nature. They were not human. They shifted and flowed, rising in a continuous, spiraling stream from the earth straight up into the starless sky, vanishing completely the moment they pierced the upper darkness. They were interlaced, a single, writhing column of flesh and spirit, their limbs and massive bodies melting into one another, twisting in a serpentine helix that mirrored the convulsions of the wind-lashed forest. They were naked, fluid entities pouring upward, weaving *within* the leaves themselves, ascending in a living pillar toward the heavens. I could never see their faces; they were smooth, featureless masks of terror.

They poured upward unceasingly, bending in great, sweeping curves, their skin a dull, sickly bronze. I stared, forcing every ounce of focus from my weary eyes, trying to find a trick, a shadow play. For a long time, I convinced myself they must dissolve instantly into the movement of the branches, proving nothing but an optical delusion. I searched desperately for evidence of reality, yet deep down, I knew the scale had shifted. The longer I looked, the more certain I became: these figures were alive, breathing, and undeniably present, even if they existed outside the laws of biology or physics.

Far from trembling, I was seized by a profound, terrifying awe, a wonder I had never known before. It felt as though I was witnessing the elemental spirits of this cursed, primordial land given form. Our intrusion had stirred the ancient slumber of the place into violent activity. We were the cause of this awakening, and my mind raced, filling to the brim with myths and legends of gods and demons worshipped by men in ages past. But before I could construct a rational explanation, an impulsion drove me forward. I crept further out on the sand, forcing myself to stand upright. The ground beneath my bare feet still hummed with a residual warmth; the wind lashed my hair and stung my face; and the roar of the river crashed against my ears with a sudden, deafening violence. These sensory inputs screamed that I was sane, that my senses were functioning correctly. And yet, there they stood—or rather, they floated—in a great spiral of terrible grace and strength, silent and majestic, overwhelming me with a deep, primal emotion of worship. I felt compelled to kneel, to bow absolutely before these beings.

Perhaps I would have fallen to my knees in reverence in another minute, had not a sudden, crushing gust of wind swept against me, knocking me sideways and nearly sending me sprawling. It shook the trance violently from me, if only for a second. It offered me a new angle, a fractured perspective. The figures still hovered there, ascending from the heart of the night, but my reason, stubborn and cruel, began to claw its way back to the surface. *It must be subjective,* I argued, fighting the paralysis. *Real, yes, but merely a projection of my own broken mind.* The moonlight and the swaying branches were working together to paint these horrors onto the mirror of my imagination, which I had foolishly projected outward. I knew I had to believe this. I gathered what courage I could and began to step forward across the open patches of sand. *By Jove,* I thought, the doubt creeping in like ice water, *is it all a hallucination? Is it merely a nightmare?* Did not my reason argue in the old, futile way, clinging to the tiny, fragile standards of the "known"?

All I know for certain is that that great column of bronze figures ascended darkly into the sky for what seemed an eternity, existing with a completeness of reality that most men take for granted. And then, without warning, they vanished. Gone. Instantly erased from the landscape.

And the moment they disappeared, the spell broke. The immediate, blinding wonder of their presence faded, and fear rushed down upon me like a freezing flood. The esoteric, bloody meaning of this lonely, haunted region flamed up within me, burning away my sanity. I began to tremble with a dread that shook my bones to the marrow. I cast a quick, frantic glance around—a look of pure horror bordering on panic—as I calculated vain, desperate ways to escape. Realizing how utterly helpless I was to effect anything meaningful, I turned and crept back silently into the tent. I lay down again upon my sandy mattress, pulling the door-curtain down low to blot out the sight of the willows in the moonlight, and buried my face as deep as possible beneath the thin blankets, praying to deaden the sound of the terrifying wind that continued to scream outside.
